source.title: LLMs on the Line: Data Determines Loss-to-Loss Scaling Laws
source.authors: Prasanna Mayilvahanan; Thaddäus Wiedemer; Sayak Mallick; Matthias Bethge; Wieland Brendel

record.file_problem: The paper text is present through its appendices, but the web extraction has NUL/corrupted characters and some figure/table formatting is degraded. It does not appear cut off or to be the wrong document.
record.tranche_reason: It tests downstream predictability from pretraining/validation loss using train-to-test loss-to-loss scaling, rather than the original compute-to-loss scaling measurement.
record.gate_note: The study reports train-to-test loss relationships, fitted shifted power laws, a high-loss fit caveat, and Table 4 areas between fitted curves under interventions. It also reports figures whose individual plotted values are not recoverable from the text; these are summarized only where the paper gives an explicit textual result. Compute-to-loss fits are used to estimate irreducible errors for loss-to-loss fits, not as reported tests of parameter/token/compute scaling or compute-optimal allocation.
record.test_reason: The paper fits train-to-test (and train-to-train) loss-to-loss shifted power laws over 6000+ checkpoints of text LMs. It checks whether downstream test loss follows predictably from pretraining or validation loss, and whether that mapping survives interventions on data, tokenizer, architecture, size, context length and optimizer. This bears on V6 with a different method from the originals. Compute-to-loss fits are used only to estimate irreducible-error terms, not reported as tests of V1–V3.
record.authors_conclusion: Essentially correct. The authors conclude that loss-to-loss scaling consistently follows shifted power laws, enabling prediction of test loss from training loss, and that pretraining data is the dominant factor shaping it. Architecture has limited impact; tokenizer, size, context length and optimizer have negligible or minor impact. Their practical recommendation is to prioritise data curation and tune architecture freely for efficiency.
record.recipe_differences: This is a loss-to-loss study, not a replication of the original compute-to-loss scaling-law measurements. It fits loss-to-loss curves using 200 to 800 checkpoints per curve, first estimating irreducible errors with compute-to-loss fits and then fitting the shifted power-law relation.
record.method_sensitivity: Pretraining data substantially changes fitted loss-to-loss curves; tokenizer, architecture, model size, context length, and tested optimization settings generally have little impact. High-loss points on some datasets fit less well. Weight tying is proposed as a possible explanation for deviations in some pretrained ablation models, but is not resolved.

fits_no_version.finding: At roughly 8B tokens, Mamba and Llama of matched size on the same data reach similar validation and test losses. Examples: 421M vs 417M on FineWeb-Edu, avg val 3.63 vs 3.58 and avg test 3.88 vs 4.04.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Transformer and state-space LMs of matched size and data reach similar held-out loss. This is close to V4, but concerns architecture family rather than shape.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267, 2025
record.problems: Individual figure values and many specific curve fits are not numerically reported in the extracted text. The work has limited checkpoints for some Hugging Face models; it says available points show discernible trends but lacks sufficient points to fit all power laws. The authors note imperfect fit in the high-loss regime and that the studied interventions are not exhaustive. The compute-to-loss fits use intermediate checkpoints as proxies for runs trained on fewer tokens, which the authors acknowledge may affect fitted shapes.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for every model, validation dataset, test task, or figure-only plotted curve in Figs. 1–2 and 4–34: the paper often reports those outcomes graphically without recoverable values, and the aggregate text results and the numeric Table 4 comparisons are retained. Table 1's individual Mamba/Llama checkpoint loss entries are not separately cataloged because the table extraction does not reliably preserve all row-to-column associations.

untested.parts: Prediction of downstream performance directly from parameters/tokens/compute. Downstream accuracy, as opposed to loss on the correct answer. Extrapolation of the loss-to-loss fit to much larger models.
Not tested. Compute-to-loss fits are only an intermediate step for irreducible error, with no reported exponents or goodness of fit.
Not tested. Models are trained to Chinchilla-optimal tokens by design, which is not a test.
Not tested directly. Depth/width variants (Table 2) are compared only on loss-to-loss curves, not on loss at fixed parameter count.
Not tested for compute-to-loss exponents. Authors only cite prior work on setup dependence and note that intermediate-checkpoint proxies may affect compute-to-loss shapes.

missing.what: Table 1 point-wise Mamba vs Llama validation and test losses at matched size and tokens. Some cells are readable despite garbled extraction (e.g. FW-Edu 421M/417M averages).
Statement that test loss follows the power law even where accuracy stays at chance (Mamba on ARC-Challenge). This bears on loss versus accuracy predictability.
Pile vs Pile-Deduped Hugging Face models fall on slightly different curves.
R² goodness-of-fit values reported in Fig. 1 are not recovered.

record.verdict_notes: Rows r09–r23 are the off-diagonal of a symmetric pairwise matrix; only r03–r08 (vs Base) are independent. 'Test loss' is loss on the correct answer (cloze), a proxy for downstream performance, not accuracy. Not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test held-out pretraining loss as a power law of parameters, tokens, or compute.
It does not test whether fits from small runs predict much larger runs.
It does not estimate compute-optimal parameter/token allocations or their growth with compute.
It compares loss-to-loss curves across architectures, but does not test whether architecture details change held-out pretraining loss only slightly at a fixed parameter count.
The experiments concern text language models and do not test other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer regimes.
Tests prediction from training/validation loss to downstream test loss; it does not test downstream prediction directly from scale or compute.

Although it varies data and training settings for loss-to-loss curves, it does not test setup dependence of the original compute-to-loss exponents or compute-optimal split, nor whether those published laws disagree.

relationships.condition: Text LMs (Llama, Mamba, GPT; 59M–12B) on the same pretraining data, across tokenizer, architecture, size, context length and optimizer changes
relationships.reason: Train-to-test loss follows shifted power laws across settings (r01), and non-data interventions shift the fitted BPB curves by only 0.00–0.03 area (r03, r05–r08, r10–r13, r18–r23).
relationships.display_finding: Train-to-test loss followed shifted power laws, while interventions other than data changes shifted fitted BPB curves by only 0.00–0.03 in area.

relation.reason: The study measures loss-to-loss relationships and how controlled changes to training settings affect them.

tranche.reason: Interventional loss-to-loss fits directly test downstream-loss predictability using a different method from the original compute-to-loss measurements.

source_check.notes: The intervention plots use common FineWeb-Edu validation loss on the x-axis, including for models pretrained elsewhere; downstream outcomes are losses, not calibrated accuracy forecasts. Table 3 additionally lists GPT-NeoX at 20B; nonconvergent Adam runs are excluded from the optimizer analysis.

statements.correction: Study-specific label: limits_scope. Pretraining-data interventions shift fitted curves; shifted power-law loss-to-loss relationships remain. Table 4: Base–Data area 0.22.
statements.problem: The factual description is correct, but the challenges label overstates this study's evidence: data changes alter the mapping without eliminating predictable loss-to-loss relationships.
